detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of the Russian Federation's active involvement in cross-border shipping and the simultaneous operation of domestic port infrastructure, the issue of regulatory documentation of delays in maritime cargo handling has become increasingly significant. This chapter develops a legal methodology for the contractual recording of deviations from the agreed schedule in transport operations falling under Russian jurisdiction. The analysis focuses on international voyages involving calls at Russian ports, including situations of legal conflict and parallel proceedings in foreign and Russian courts. The study examines inconsistencies between international standards (BIMCO, LMAA) and Russian law, the evidentiary role of documents such as NOR, SOF, and LoP, the admissibility of electronic evidence, and the legal qualification of demurrage. The chapter substantiates the need for structured rider clauses specifying the applicable law, arbitration forum, digital documentation procedures, and anti-suit provisions. The proposed methodology aims to reduce legal uncertainty, ensure the reproducibility of contractual arrangements, and strengthen the arbitration infrastructure in transportrelated disputes.

title: Priced Out: Housing Costs, Gendered Migration, and the Geography of Crime in China
affiliations: , Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management, Peking University - School of Economics and INSE at Peking University

detail.title: Priced Out: Housing Costs, Gendered Migration, and the Geography of Crime in China
detail.abstract: Housing-price shocks can reallocate crime across space by changing who moves. Using millions of Chinese court judgments from 2014-2018, we construct city-level measures of criminal participation and show that rising housing costs reshape the geography of crime, with the largest responses in male-perpetrated and male-intensive offenses. We argue that marriage-market norms place disproportionate home-purchase burdens on men; as a result, higher housing costs induce male-skewed out-migration from expensive cities, altering local sex ratios and the supply of potential offenders. Instrumenting housing prices with land prices and differential exposure to regional housing cycles, we find that a 1% increase in housing prices reduces crime in origin cities by about 1.3%, with partially offsetting increases in destination cities. A spatial-equilibrium model calibrated to Chinese migration and crime data identifies two elasticities governing aggregate effects: how criminal payoffs vary with offender concentration and with the scale of the legal economy. The calibration implies weak effects of offender dispersion but strong effects of local economic scale, suggesting that male-selective outflows primarily relocate crime across cities while modestly reducing aggregate criminal participation as high-cost origins contract.

title: Reintegrating Equity into Money Creation: Toward an Ex-Ante Distribution Framework for Reducing Global Inequality

detail.title: Reintegrating Equity into Money Creation: Toward an Ex-Ante Distribution Framework for Reducing Global Inequality
detail.abstract:
The persistence of poverty and inequality is one of the major paradoxes of the contemporary economy: global wealth creation has never been so high, yet income disparities are widening within and between countries. Traditional redistribution mechanisms – taxation, social transfers, support programmes – struggle to correct these imbalances, mainly because they occur after the production of wealth, and remain dependent on budgetary, political and institutional constraints. This structural limitation reveals a central question that is too often dismissed: to what extent can economic justice really emerge from a system where equity is not integrated into the process of money creation itself?

The Folahan model proposes a conceptual alternative based on a partial reorientation of seigniorage towards the direct and transparent financing of economic opportunities for individuals. Rather than redistributing ex post, it introduces an initial, conditional and productive distribution mechanism, aligned with the objectives of inclusive growth. This framework aims to strengthen economic autonomy, reduce asymmetries in access to capital, and create a systemic foundation of social resilience. By putting equity back at the heart of the monetary architecture, the Folahan model paves the way for renewed thinking about the foundations of the fight against poverty on a global scale.

detail.title: Axiomatic Foundations of Bayesian Persuasion

detail.abstract: In this paper, we study axiomatic foundations of Bayesian persuasion, where a principal (i.e., sender) delegates the task of choice making after informing a biased agent (i.e., receiver) about the payoff relevant uncertain state (see, e.g., Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011)). Our characterizations involve novel models of Bayesian persuasion, where the principal can steer the agent's bias after acquiring costly information. Importantly, we provide an elicitation method using only observable menu-choice data of the principal, which shows how to construct the principal's subjective costs of acquiring information even when he anticipates managing the agent's bias.

title: Youth Unemployment & Job Crisis: A Situation Analysis and Way forward
affiliations: Chittagong Independent University

detail.title: Youth Unemployment & Job Crisis: A Situation Analysis and Way forward
detail.abstract: Youth unemployment in Bangladesh constitutes a persistent structural challenge that undermines inclusive growth and the effective utilization of the country's demographic dividend. Although educational attainment has increased over the past decade, labour market absorption has not kept pace, resulting in rising unemployment, underemployment, and high NEET rates among young people. Existing literature attributes these outcomes to skills mismatch, limited diversification of the economy, weak coordination across employment-related institutions, and significant genderbased barriers. This paper conducts a situation analysis grounded in recent empirical studies, labour force data, and policy reports to assess the underlying determinants of the youth job crisis. It further examines the implications of governance constraints, labour market informality, and post-pandemic disruptions. Based on the evidence reviewed, the paper outlines strategic policy directions, emphasizing strengthened TVET systems, improved labour market information frameworks, targeted gender-responsive interventions, and enhanced multi-agency coordination. The findings underscore the need for comprehensive and sustained reform to ensure productive youth engagement in Bangladesh's labour market.

title: An Author Perspective for Next-Generation Cybersecurity

detail.title: An Author Perspective for Next-Generation Cybersecurity
detail.abstract: Cybersecurity operates in environments shaped by heavy-tailed behavior, adversarial manipulation, concept drift, and heterogeneous uncertainty. Yet most current evaluation tools-accuracy, global ROC/AUC, aggregate anomaly scores, and classical p-values-treat evidence as if it were epistemically homogeneous across the decision space. This author perspective introduces Zonal Epistemic Statistics (EZS) as a conceptual foundation for stability-aware, interpretability-oriented cybersecurity analytics. EZS decomposes the evidence landscape into epistemic zones-Trusted, Plausible, and Foot (high-variability) regions-defined through standard-error-based partitions and refined with tools such as partition-wise pvalues, Robust Adjusted Mean Estimates (RAME), Robust Adjusted Mean Intervals (RAMI), and Zone-Restricted ROC (ZR-ROC) (Raham, 2025a; 2025b). By localizing evidence in these zones, EZS reveals where threat signals originate, how classifier reliability varies, and where adversaries are most likely to exploit instability. This perspective argues that EZS provides a natural epistemic layer above classical statistics, offering a more credible, drift-sensitive, and adversarially aware framework for next-generation cybersecurity.

title: Economic Guarantees of Security

detail.abstract: This article introduces and theoretically substantiates the concept of economic guarantees of security — a new class of international commitments aimed at preventing aggression and ensuring the implementation of peace treaties. The traditional security system relies on political and military deterrence, while the economic factor usually plays a reactive role through sanctions and compensation after conflict (Baldwin, 1997). A different approach is proposed: the use of pre-established economic consequences for violations of agreements, and, conversely, material incentives for maintaining peace (Rozenfeld, 2024). The key idea is the institutionalization of economic guarantees in the form of “special sections” of international agreements that define concrete financial enforcement mechanisms: funds, bonds, insurance instruments, and asset freezes based on predetermined criteria (Kunreuther & Michel-Kerjan, 2009). This solution makes the security system economically enforceable, turning war into a financially disadvantageous action (Fearon, 1995).

title: Distributional Consequences of Climate Risk: A Review of Heterogeneous-Agent Macroeconomic Models

detail.title: Distributional Consequences of Climate Risk: A Review of Heterogeneous-Agent Macroeconomic Models

detail.abstract: Climate change generates heterogeneous macroeconomic impacts through physical damages, transition dynamics, and financial channels, with important implications for inequality and welfare. This review provides a comparative synthesis of recent macroeconomic modelling approaches to climate risk, drawing on approximately fifty studies spanning heterogeneous-agent models, integrated assessment models, macro-finance frameworks, and agent-based approaches. Rather than cataloguing findings, the review systematically contrasts how different modelling choices shape conclusions regarding transmission mechanisms, distributional outcomes, and policy effectiveness. Across studies, physical climate risks disproportionately affect income-and location-vulnerable households through productivity losses and exposure to extreme events, while transition risks operate primarily via energy prices, sectoral reallocation, and asset revaluation. Heterogeneous-agent models consistently reveal larger distributional effects than representative-agent frameworks, whereas macro-finance models highlight amplification through credit constraints and financial instability. The literature diverges on the welfare effects of carbon pricing: some studies identify regressive short-run impacts, while others find that revenue recycling and redistribution can render mitigation policies welfare-stabilising or welfare-improving. These disagreements are shown to stem primarily from differences in assumptions regarding market completeness, financial structure, and policy design. The review identifies areas of convergence, including the amplification of climate damages by inequality and the inadequacy of aggregate welfare metrics, as well as persistent gaps related to financial-sector integration, uncertainty representation, spatial granularity, and the treatment of developing economies. Overall, the evidence demonstrates that climate policy evaluation is inherently distributional and model-dependent, underscoring the need for integrated frameworks that jointly capture heterogeneity, uncertainty, and policy realism.

title: Environmental Damage from Sunken Vessels and Legal Mechanisms for Its Compensation

detail.abstract: This article examines the legal nature of environmental risks arising from sunken vessels and decommissioned floating objects remaining in aquatic environments of the Russian Federation. The research analyzes the regulatory framework governing shipowners' obligations to raise and remove sunken property, including the Russian Merchant Shipping Code, the Water Code, and environmental protection legislation. Special attention is given to judicial practice affirming the presumption of environmental damage caused by abandoned submerged vessels and classifying the owner's inaction as unlawful. The study also reviews applicable damage-assessment methodologies, including the official methodology of the Ministry of Natural Resources, and discusses challenges related to evidentiary standards, causation, and the implementation of the "polluter pays" principle. Based on legislative analysis, court rulings, and doctrinal sources, the article formulates practical recommendations for shipowners and maritime operators.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), including types of AI/ML tools, use cases, challenges & opportunities, solutions, and how these factors impact the stability of the financial system in the context of credit risk management. The uniqueness of this paper lies in its synthesis of multiple perspectives on the application of AI in this field. It is based on a selection of relevant research papers, industry reports, and regulatory reports from Google Scholar, SSRN, ResearchGate, McKinsey & Company, Deloitte, GARP, BIS, FSB, and the FED. The paper addresses the gap in integrating ongoing research in credit risk management, adoption of AI, regulatory challenges, and the solutions being discussed to address those. It also discusses the policy implications and future direction of research in this context. Ongoing research shows that even though AI is resolving the limitations of traditional models through the application of artificial intelligence and various ML models, AI has its own challenges, as the regulators and users find it difficult to understand the black-box nature of these AI tools and models, where there is a growing scope for further research.

detail.title: Does Belonging to a Farmer Organization Improve Extension Access? A Study of Cocoa Farmers in Fako Division, Cameroon
detail.abstract: The literature on farmer-organization membership and access to agricultural extension services (AES) reports mixed findings, motivating further empirical study. This paper examines whether membership in farmer organizations (FOs) improves access to AES among cocoa farmers in Fako Division, Cameroon. Using structured questionnaires, primary data were collected from 396 randomly selected cocoa farmers. Descriptive statistics were first used to summarise sample characteristics (including FO membership status and gender) and the distribution of AES access.To address the specific objectives, a chi-square test was used to evaluate the bivariate association between FO membership and AES access, and a binary logistic regression was used to assess the effect of FO membership on AES access while controlling for education, farm size, age, and gender. Results show a large disparity in AES access: 83.5% of FO members reported access to extension services compared to 34.8% of non-members (difference ≈ 49 percentage points). The chi-square test confirmed a strong association between FO membership and AES access (χ² = 57.82, p < .001). The logistic regression model was statistically significant, χ²(5) = 116.45, p < .001, with a Nagelkerke R² of 0.42, indicating that the predictors explained about 42% of the variance in AES access. FO membership was the strongest predictor (B = 1.84, SE = 0.28, OR = 6.30, p < .001), meaning members were over six times more likely to access AES than non-members. Years of education also had a positive and significant effect on AES access (B = 0.11, SE = 0.04, OR = 1.12, p = .008), while farm size showed a marginal effect (B = 0.07, SE = 0.03, OR = 1.07, p = .089). Age (B = –0.01, p = .215) and gender (coded 1 = Male; B = 0.15, p = .495) were not significant predictors. The Conclusion was that membership in farmer organizations substantially increases cocoa farmers’ likelihood of accessing agricultural extension services in Fako Division, and education further improves farmers’ ability to obtain those services. Based on these findings, we recommend strengthening of farmer organizations, promoting inclusive membership, and formally integrating FOs into extension delivery systems to improve the equity and effectiveness of service access.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how income level and gender shape individuals' perceptions of the major life expenses that families commonly plan for in India-higher education, weddings, housing, raising children and retirement. Primary data were collected through a structured survey in which respondents first reported their household income bracket and gender, and then estimated the average cost of each life event for a household of their own socioeconomic class. Responses were analysed across five income groups to compare mean estimates, variability and gender differences. The results show a clear upward progression in perceived costs as income increases, with the largest shifts occurring between low-income and lower-middle-income households, showing rising aspirations as economic status improves. Gender differences were consistent across most categories: men tended to estimate higher costs for weddings, property purchase and retirement, while women-especially in lower-income groups-reported higher expected spending on raising children. High within-group variation, particularly for housing and retirement estimates, indicates that financial expectations are shaped by diverse personal experiences, social norms and local market exposure. Overall, the findings highlight that both income and gender strongly influence how people imagine their financial futures.

detail.abstract: We present a new approach to formulating and solving heterogeneous agent models with aggregate risk. We replace the cross-sectional distribution with low-dimensional prices as state variables and let agents learn equilibrium price dynamics directly from simulated paths. To do so, we introduce a structural reinforcement learning (SRL) method which treats prices via simulation while exploiting agents’ structural knowledge of their own individual dynamics. Our SRL method yields a general and highly efficient global solution method for heterogeneous agent models that sidesteps the Master equation and handles models traditional methods struggle with, like those with nontrivial market-clearing conditions. We illustrate the approach in the Krusell-Smith model, the Huggett model with aggregate shocks, and a HANK model with a forward-looking Phillips curve, all of which we solve globally within minutes.

detail.abstract: This paper takes the logical closed loop of talent, private economy, and common prosperity as the research object. Combining historical allusions and practical cases, it sorts out the symbiotic relationship between the fate of top talents and the soil of the times, analyzes the value contribution and development concerns of the private economy in the reform and opening-up drive, explores the balanced path of activating capital vitality while adhering to the bottom line of fairness, and puts forward practical suggestions for joint efforts through legal protection, policy guidance, and social governance. It demonstrates the core significance of the positive cycle of the three to national reform and era development.

detail.abstract: The contemporary battlefield-defined by the mass employment of FPV drones, multispectral sensor suites, integrated ISR systems, and precision-guided munitions-has produced an unprecedented level of informational transparency in which tactical medical evacuation no longer conforms to classical doctrinal assumptions. Drawing on field observations from Ukrainian units (2022-2025) and analytical modeling conducted in MATLAB, this study introduces a new conceptual framework that treats battlefield transparency as a probabilistic process dynamically updated through a Bayesian mechanism. A connectivity parameter (C) is proposed to quantify the degree of coordination among friendly measures aimed at reducing sensor exposure (EW, smoke and thermal screens, maneuver, deception), thereby determining a unit's ability to generate short-lived "windows of reduced transparency." Modeling demonstrated that under conditions of persistent aerial surveillance and dense sensor saturation, evacuation risk becomes sharply nonlinear, while Bayesian updates consistently shift the expected transparency toward higher values, rendering most traditional evacuation scenarios operationally infeasible. Only at sufficiently high levels of connectivity (C ≥ 0.6-0.7) do tactical conditions emerge that are compatible with relatively safe evacuation. Based on this framework, FIRE-FORM v1.0 is introduced as a universal field tool for rapid "evacuate / do not evacuate" decision-making, integrating transparency, connectivity, and Bayesian likelihood into a single composite risk index. This approach establishes a new analytical paradigm for medical support in hyper-transparent battlespaces and offers a foundation for the development of adaptive doctrines and decision-making algorithms suited to technologically advanced modern warfare.

title: Rainfall Variability, Irrigation, and Price Support: Mediating Agricultural Resilience in India
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Management Kashipur

detail.title: Rainfall Variability, Irrigation, and Price Support: Mediating Agricultural Resilience in India
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of rainfall deviations on agricultural productivity in India, focusing on paddy and wheat yields using a district-level panel dataset spanning nearly two decades (2001-2017). Employing a Standardized Rainfall Anomaly and other rainfall variability indicators, the study evaluates the e!ects of rainfall shocks and assesses the mitigating role of irrigation and the influence of Minimum Support Prices (MSP) on agricultural outcomes. Results reveal that negative rainfall deviations significantly reduce paddy yields, while wheat yields exhibit a comparatively weaker response. Irrigation e!ectively cushions the adverse e!ects of rainfall deficits, but diminishing marginal returns highlight the limits of its e!ectiveness under severe drought conditions. Additionally, MSP positively influences yields, suggesting that supportive pricing policies can enhance agricultural resilience by promoting input use and farm investments. The findings underscore the necessity for robust climate-resilient policies, including sustainable water management, improved irrigation infrastructure, climate sensitive price support, and adaptive cropping practices. By providing empirical evidence on the intricate relationship between climate variability and agricultural performance, this study informs targeted interventions to enhance food security and safeguard farmer livelihoods in the face of increasing climatic uncertainties.

detail.title: Patent Rights and Cumulative Innovation

detail.abstract: This article reviews theoretical and empirical evidence on how patent rights shape cumulative innovation. Theoretically, models highlight a trade-off: strong patents can spur first-generation inventions yet block follow-on research, with outcomes depending on patent length, breadth, validity, licensing institutions, and technology characteristics. Empirically, quasi-experiments exploiting random invalidation, oppositions, IP restrictions on research tools, and disclosure shocks reveal substantial, heterogeneous effects on subsequent patenting, scientific publications, and R&D investment. The overall picture rejects one-size-fits-all prescriptions: in complex technologies and where licensing fails, strong rights often hinder cumulative innovation, while in discrete or high-cost domains they remain an important driver of inventive activity.

title: A Comprehensive Analysis of the Legitimacy Boundaries of Professor Zhao Hong's Proposal for Sealing Public Order Violation Records at Peking University Based on Marxist Jurisprudence and Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law

detail.title: A Comprehensive Analysis of the Legitimacy Boundaries of Professor Zhao Hong's Proposal for Sealing Public Order Violation Records at Peking University Based on Marxist Jurisprudence and Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law

keywords: Sealing Of Public Security Violation Records
Xi Jinping Thought On The Rule Of Law

detail.abstract: The newly revised Law of the People's Republic of China on Penalties for Public Order Violations introduces a "system for sealing public order violation records," with the sealing of records for acts such as drug use sparking intense public debate. Zhao Hong, a researcher at Peking University Law School, has systematically articulated several key arguments in multiple media outlets in defence of the sealing system. These include: "Drug use constitutes an administrative offence rather than a criminal act"; "Sealing records embodies the legal system's civilised approach to tolerance for error and rehabilitation"; and "Opposition to governing society through ancient-style branding methods akin to facial tattooing." This article meticulously reconstructs his principal arguments while introducing Marxist legal theory, Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law and key anti-drug directives, formal logic and argumentation theory, alongside comparative Western jurisprudential experience concerning "criminal record sealing/expungement" to conduct a multidimensional critical analysis of his discourse. The research indicates: on the one hand, Zhao Hong's conceptual distinctions between "public order offences versus criminal offences" and "sealing versus expungement" possess a certain enlightening significance, and formally align with contemporary international trends towards "stigma removal and reintegration promotion". On the other hand, his argumentation exhibits significant blind spots in terms of class analysis, the people's stance, and the overall security perspective: it inadequately exposes the class structures and inequalities underlying drug issues; lacks a holistic grasp of the tension between "people's security" and "individual rights"; and insufficiently internalises Xi Jinping's requirements for "zero tolerance" in drug control, coordinating security and development, and adhering to bottom-line thinking (You Quanrong, 2023; Xi Jinping, 2015; Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, 2020). Logically, it extrapolates universal sealing from a minority of minor offences and counters public security anxieties by occupying the moral high ground of "modern rule of law civilisation," exhibiting a structural bias of "substituting risk analysis with moralising rhetoric." From a comparative law perspective, Western legal systems predominantly adopt a refined "tieredconditional-exceptional" model, excluding acts severely endangering public safety from blanket sealing while supplementing this with rigorous procedures and ex post facto review mechanisms. This paper ultimately proposes that for the sealing system of public security violation records to embody the humanitarian concerns of socialist rule of law within the Chinese context while aligning with the overarching national security outlook and the practical logic of the "people's war" on drugs, it must introduce mechanisms such as tiered sealing, strict exceptions, procedural participation, and dynamic assessment at both legislative and discursive levels. Concurrently, it must theoretically return to the people-centred stance and practice-oriented approach emphasised by Marxist jurisprudence and Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law.

title: Intelagencyism: AI, Learning and Cognitive Sovereignty in the Postdigital Condition

detail.abstract: The postdigital learner emerges within a cognitive ecology in which artificial intelligence functions not merely as a tool but as a constitutive layer of thought itself. The friction between algorithmic cognition and institutional schooling signals not a failure of the student but the exhaustion of institutional education as the privileged locus of knowledge production. Intelagencyism emerges as a learning theory that redefines learning as an ontological act of cognitive sovereignty, enacted through symbiotic entanglement with AI yet irreducible to algorithmic control. It resists the humanist fantasy of mastery while aligning with posthumanist critique, recognizing that learning arises from entanglements with technologies, ecologies, and cultural environments. Drawing on philosophical traditions and contemporary critiques of algorithmic power, Intelagencyism proposes that AI can amplify attention, sustain intrinsic motivation, and support learner autonomy. Simultaneously, it warns against the risks of surveillance capitalism and algorithmic closure, insisting that AI must be governed through reciprocal relations of agency rather than optimization imperatives. Intelagencyism positions postdigital learners' refusal to participate in institutional forms as the incipient site of a new subjectivity. By grounding learning in the localization and naturalization of experience in soil, language, community, and environment, augmented by AI as a cognitive partner, the theory decenters the human subject while restoring agency. In this sense, Intelagencyism offers a framework for postdigital learning commensurate with the crises of the twenty-first century.

title: Social Pressure and Decision-Making: Evidence of Referee Bias in 2.3 Million NCAA Basketball Player-Game Observations
affiliations: Texas Tech University

detail.title: Social Pressure and Decision-Making: Evidence of Referee Bias in 2.3 Million NCAA Basketball Player-Game Observations
detail.abstract: How does social pressure affect expert judgment? I exploit the COVID-19 crowd shutdown as a natural experiment to measure the effect of social pressure on highly trained decision-makers—NCAA basketball referees. Using 2.3 million player-game observations from 2005–2025, I find that referee bias toward home teams shrinks by 40–45% when crowds are absent. In normal seasons, home players receive favorable treatment from referees: they commit fewer fouls and attempt more free throws than away players in the same game. These advantages decline substantially during the 2020–2021 season without crowds. Critically, the effect appears only in subjective referee-dependent outcomes (fouls, free throws), not in objective performance measures (rebounds, assists), isolating the behavioral mechanism. The findings demonstrate that even experienced professionals operating under institutional monitoring exhibit systematic bias when exposed to partisan social pressure.

title: Speculation and Resale in Emission Trading Systems
affiliations: RMIT University

detail.title: Speculation and Resale in Emission Trading Systems
detail.abstract: Emissions trading systems (ETS) typically rely on multi-unit auctions for the initial allocation of permits and on secondary markets for subsequent reallocation. This paper studies how the presence of a frictionless secondary market and speculative bidders affects bidding behavior, revenue, and the distribution of surplus in uniform-price permit auctions, and how banking and auction frequency can be used to manage demand uncertainty. Within a standard framework, we show that the option to trade later in a competitive secondary market weakens firms’ incentives to bid aggressively in the primary auction: equilibrium bid schedules shift downward and the range of equilibrium uniform prices is compressed relative to a benchmark without resale. When the primary allocation is inefficient, a competitive secondary market restores efficiency but creates rents for initial low-valuation winners, including pure speculators; these rents mirror auction revenue that the regulator could have collected under a more efficient primary allocation. We then introduce a simple two-period setting with banking and show that allowing firms to carry permits forward raises their effective willingness to pay in early auctions and enlarges the set of efficient allocations implementable directly through the auction schedule, reducing the minimal secondary trading required to reach the efficient allocation. A numerical example illustrates how demand reduction, speculative entry, and banking interact and highlights that frequent auctions with banking can substitute for some of the risk-sharing role otherwise left to secondary markets and intermediaries.

detail.abstract: This chapter investigates whether and how digital tax infrastructure in Kenya, Ghana, and Djibouti can be harnessed to mobilise resources for children's welfare, in line with states' obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child to use the maximum available resources for the progressive realisation of rights. It applies a child-sensitive fiscal framework that measures effectiveness, efficiency, and equity against two enabling conditions: that revenue gains from digitalisation are directed to childfocused spending, and that households with children are protected from disproportionate burdens. UNICEF's Public Finance for Children dimensions are used to structure the assessment. The study employs a mixed-methods comparative design. In Kenya, fieldwork in Wakulima and Gikomba markets captured the lived realities of informal sector parents whose businesses run almost entirely on mobile money yet remain outside the tax net. In Ghana, institutional interviews explored the integration of the Ghana Card into tax and social protection systems. In Djibouti, interviews with government officials examined the domestic application of world-class data infrastructure. In each case, evidence was analysed through the indirect pathway (digitalisation expanding fiscal space) and the direct pathway (digital systems delivering benefits to children). formalisation to tangible services such as subsidised school fees or health access. Fourth, to establish high-level coordination mechanisms with authority to mandate integration across agencies. Fifth, to regulate private intermediaries to guarantee data access, low-cost social transfers, and service standards in the public interest. Sixth, to build trust with a public child-sensitivity scorecard tracking adequacy, efficiency, equity, and effectiveness. Finally, to align donor support to integrated, child-sensitive fiscal reforms rather than isolated technical builds. UNICEF's role is central to advancing these reforms. As a broker, fiscal guardian, designer of inclusive access, evidence-maker, and communicator of results, UNICEF can ensure that digitalisation strengthens the fiscal social contract in ways that see the child, fund the child, and reach the child. The evidence, analysis, and recommendations in this chapter show that child-sensitive digital fiscal reform is achievable, but it requires deliberate sequencing, political coalition-building, and a commitment to transparency. Without this, digitalisation risks reinforcing exclusion rather than advancing the rights and welfare of the next generation.

title: Narrowing industry wage premiums and the decline in the gender wage gap
affiliations: Banque de France, INSEAD and INSEAD

detail.title: Narrowing industry wage premiums and the decline in the gender wage gap
detail.abstract: The gender gap in firm wage premiums is well documented, but evidence on its evolution over time and its contribution to declining gender wage gaps remains mixed. Using comprehensive employer–employee data from France, we find that 20% of the reduction in the gender hourly wage gap between 2002 and 2019 can be attributed to a decline in the between-firm component of the gender gap in firm wage premiums. However, our analysis shows that this reduction is not driven by improvements in women’s relative position in the firm wage premium ladder. We find no evidence that, conditional on workers’ skills, women have become more likely to move into higher-paying firms or industries, or that newer cohorts of women are better represented in these segments. Instead, the narrowing is primarily driven by broader changes in the distribution of firm wage premiums, specifically through a compression of industry-specific premium differentials. These findings highlight how structural changes in the economy can affect gender wage gaps even in the absence of changes in women’s relative labor market position.

title: Committee Elections with Candidate AttributeConstraints
affiliations: Ocean University of China, Ocean University of China, Shandong University and Ocean University of China

detail.title: Committee Elections with Candidate AttributeConstraints
detail.abstract: The Mixture of Experts (MoE) is a neural network architecture which is widely used in fields such as natural language processing (such as large language models, multilingual translation), computer vision (such as medical image analysis, multi-modal learning), and recommendation systems. A core problem of the MoE is how to select an expert assigned to a specific task among all experts.This problem can be transformed into an election problem where each expert is a candidate and the winner of election (a candidate or some candidates) is the expert who is assigned to the task by considering the votes.We study a variant of committee elections from the perspective of computational complexity. Given a set of candidates, each possessing a set of attributes and a profit value, and a set of constraints specified as propositional logical expressions on the attributes, the task is to select a committee of k candidates that satisfies all constraints and whose total profit meets a given threshold. Regarding the classical complexity, we design two polynomial time algorithms for two special conditions and provide some NP-hardness results.Moreover, we examine the parameterized complexity and get some FPT, W[1]-hard and para-NP-hard results.

title: Cultivating the disaster: Latifundia and natural hazards in pre-industrial Sicily
affiliations: University of Siena - Department of Economics and Statistics

detail.title: Cultivating the disaster: Latifundia and natural hazards in pre-industrial Sicily
detail.abstract: This paper examines how extractive land institutions shape long-term environmental vulnerability by promoting land-use patterns that amplify natural hazards. Focusing on pre-industrial Sicily, a canonical case of latifundia and grain monoculture, this study gathers a novel municipality-level dataset linking historical land-use data (1838-1929) with landslide records from 1838 to 1959. Using Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood and probit models with detailed geographic and climatic controls, results show that grain cultivation, the cornerstone of the Sicilian latifundia system, robustly increased landslide risk: a 1% rise in grain area raised expected landslide events by about 0.47%. Decomposition exercises reveal that the positive association for vineyards reflects later crop adaptation in hazard-prone areas rather than a direct causal effect. Consistent with predatory expansion onto marginal land, the effects of grain cultivation are significantly stronger in municipalities with low soil suitability. These results highlight a concrete channel through which extractive institutions generate persistent environmental externalities, embedding disaster risk into the landscape.

title: Predictive Volatility of Option Returns under Autocorrelated Stock Returns

detail.title: Predictive Volatility of Option Returns under Autocorrelated Stock Returns

detail.abstract: Most option pricing models are extensions based on the assumption that stock prices follow a geometric Brownian motion (GBM hereafter), for instance, by adding jump components. The GBM framework, characterized by a constant drift, implies zero autocorrelation of stock returns between periods. In contrast, Lo and Wang (1995) adopt the trending Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (O-U hereafter) process, wherein the drift is a linear function of ln(St), rather than a constant, to accommodate the condition of constant autocorrelated stock returns, which also serves as the basic framework of this study.

title: Transforming Extraction into Protection: From Global Tax Drainage to a Global Social Protection Fund
affiliations: University of Nairobi

detail.title: Transforming Extraction into Protection: From Global Tax Drainage to a Global Social Protection Fund
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the global tax system perpetuates colonial patterns of wealth extraction from Africa, directly undermining states' capacity to provide social protection, and proposes a transformative Global Social Protection Fund (GSPF) as systematic restitution. Drawing on historical analysis and contemporary data, it demonstrates how base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS), illicit financial flows (IFFs), and tax incentives systematically drain resources that could finance social programmes. Sub-Saharan Africa loses approximately $88.6 billion annually to IFFs, representing 3.7 percent of its GDP, whilst 98 percent of people living in extreme poverty have no access to adequate social protection. Using case studies from Djibouti's free zones and Angola's oil sector, the paper describes how tax incentives; reducing corporate rates to as low as 6% in Angola, directly constrain social expenditure whilst facilitating profit extraction through sophisticated mechanisms including royalty payments, management fees, and transfer pricing manipulation. The paper traces these contemporary extraction mechanisms to their colonial origins, revealing how racialised assumptions about fiscal capacity established institutional frameworks that continue to disadvantage African countries in international tax governance. The analysis demonstrates that between 1980 and 2018, Sub-Saharan Africa lost $1.3 trillion to illicit financial flows, roughly equal to the continent's current GDP and far exceeding development assistance received over the same period. In response, the paper proposes a Global Social Protection Fund financed through coordinated withholding taxes on the very transactions that currently facilitate extraction.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a simple framework for analysing sovereign risk through the lens of civilizational dynamics. Rather than starting from debt ratios or spreads, the Sovereign Risk under Civilizational Dynamics (SRC) approach begins from five dimensions of a state–society system: energy or productive capacity, structural burden, meaning field cohesion, adaptive capacity and institutional lock–in. Observable macroeconomic, institutional and survey indicators are mapped into two composite objects—a civilizational capacity curve and a systemic burden curve—and a structural imbalance index is defined as the difference between them. When the burden curve persistently exceeds the capacity curve, the system is said to be in an overloaded regime. Using only publicly available data from sources such as the World Bank, IMF, OECD and governance and values surveys, the paper constructs SRC indices for France over 1995–2025. The French case exhibits a robust energy base but a steadily rising structural burden, weakening cohesion and increasing institutional lock–in. The resulting imbalance index displays patterns that are consistent with known episodes of sovereign stress and with a medium-term drift into a persistent overloaded regime. The paper does not offer point forecasts of spreads. Instead, it shows how SRC can serve as a transparent “scenario engine” that organises qualitative narratives about fiscal policy, demographics and politics into structured assessments of sovereign risk. The conclusion outlines limitations of the approach and suggests directions for multi-country and more formal econometric extensions.

title: Monetary Theory of Production: Revolutionary or Not Microfounded?
affiliations: Center for Social Studies, University of Coimbra

detail.title: Monetary Theory of Production: Revolutionary or Not Microfounded?
detail.abstract: The paper questions the thesis that Keynes's theoretical contributions lacked ‘solid microfoundations'. First, it contributes to the perception that Keynes's theory does not equal Keynesian theory by emphasising the role of money and arguing that: (i) (Neo)Classical economics is not a special case of the General Theory and (ii) when dealing with Keynes's theory, we should use the term Monetary Theory of Production. The article then provides a brief historical overview of what Denis (2016, ‘Microfoundations.' Review of Political Economy 28 (1): 134-152) called the ‘microfoundation project'. It seeks its definition in the New Classical Macroeconomics literature of the 1970s and, more importantly, presents its core components: optimisation, market clearing, the representative agent and the rational expectations hypothesis. In light of the overall inadequacy of this project, the article proposes new (and tentative) criteria based on which we ought to identify new microfoundations: agents' abilities and behaviours, as well as the institutional environment in which they act. Based on the new criteria advanced and a critique of the core components of the microfoundation project, the article proceeds to investigate whether Keynes's MTP lacks solid microfoundations and explores the role played by money and time in Keynes’s conceptions of micro-behaviour.

title: Environmental contradictions in the EU accession process: lessons from a lithium mining project in Serbia

detail.title: Environmental contradictions in the EU accession process: lessons from a lithium mining project in Serbia
detail.abstract: The EU’s ambition to achieve climate neutrality by 2050, alongside its pursuit of strategic autonomy in critical raw materials such as lithium, often finds itself at odds with its own environmental regulations, binding on both member states and candidates. Serbia – a candidate for EU membership and a country possessing substantial lithium deposits – epitomises this inherent tension, enabling an analysis that extends beyond the confines of a single national jurisdiction. The paper contends that the feasibility of lithium extraction in the EU candidate countries entails the subordination of the Union’s legal standards to its overarching economic and strategic imperatives.

title: The Role and Function of Algorithmic Digitization in the Miseducation Processing of Ancient Histories: The Case of the Moors and Contemporary Corrective Scholarship
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: The Role and Function of Algorithmic Digitization in the Miseducation Processing of Ancient Histories: The Case of the Moors and Contemporary Corrective Scholarship
detail.abstract: This paper examines how algorithmic digitization perpetuates and accelerates centuries-old processes of historical miseducation. Using the popular distortions surrounding "the Moors" as a primary case study, I demonstrate how search algorithms, media casting decisions, and digital knowledge curation create selfreinforcing cycles that entrench historical falsehoods while marginalizing corrective scholarship. The paper introduces the concept of "algorithmic digitization" as operating on dual levels: (1) the systematic encoding of history through media representation and casting choices, and (2) the algorithmic curation of historical knowledge through search engines and digital repositories. Drawing on empirical data from thirty scholarly papers posted to SSRN (15,000+ downloads, zero scholarly comments), I demonstrate how the same algorithmic mechanisms that bury historical narratives operate on contemporary scholarship attempting corrective work. The paper reveals a troubling paradox: artificial intelligence enables independent scholars to produce rigorous corrective historical work at unprecedented scale, yet AI assistance itself becomes grounds for professional marginalization. More troubling still, academic institutions deploy AI for peer review gatekeeping while stigmatizing its use for knowledge production by non-credentialed scholars. This reveals algorithmic digitization as fundamentally about power protection rather than knowledge accuracy. The paper concludes that miseducation processing is not a relic of past textbook committees but an active, accelerating phenomenon in the digital age, with profound implications for democratic access to historical knowledge and the future of scholarly legitimacy.

title: Safety Envelopes and Continuous Assurance for Updates and Postmarket Surveillance in Digital Mental Health Technologies

detail.abstract: Digital mental health technologies (DMHTs) increasingly function as continuously updated services, yet many regulatory and procurement pathways still evaluate them as comparatively static products, creating a governance gap at the point where change, context, and risk interact most sharply. This perspective integrates recent regulatory developments and emerging evidence-change control, significant-change disclosure, evidence thresholds, adverse-event handling, and responsibilities for post-market surveillance (PMS)-into a single lifecycle governance proposal for both SaMD-classified and "adjacent" mental-health apps that influence outcomes through content, interface, or coaching behaviors. I argue that the most practical and future-resilient regulatory unit is not "the version" but a bounded Safety Envelope paired with Continuous Assurance, so that predetermined change control plans (PCCPs) become auditable commitments that constrain updates, specify evidence, and mandate real-world monitoring and rollback. To operationalize this, I propose SECA (Safety Envelope and Continuous Assurance) as a low-cost, implementable model that couples a change taxonomy, a minimum evidence bundle, a machine-readable change manifest, and a shared escalation pathway that includes platforms (app stores) as enforceable "last-mile" gatekeepers. SECA is calibrated for the EU/UK, US, and India by aligning with existing PMS and vigilance structures while explicitly incorporating mental-health-specific context triggers, including population vulnerability, language and cultural shifts, and interaction design effects that can plausibly alter cognition, affect, and behavior.

detail.title: The Electoral Consequences of AI Adoption: Evidence from US Elections
detail.abstract: What are the impacts of AI adoption on electoral outcomes? Unlike previous research on the electoral consequences of automation, we show that AI can benefit the political left. This occurs as a result of both economic voting and composition effects in response to AI adoption. Using data from the U.S. presidential elections (2020 and 2024) and a novel measure of AI labor market tightness and a shift-share design, we show that: i) The vote share for Democrats increases as voters swing to the left, reflecting improving local economic conditions. This economic voting effect is driven by ideological moderates. ii) AI adoption manifests in job creation, which attracts more educated workers, who are more likely to be left-leaning. This composition effect also benefits Democrats. We show that AI as not just an economic force but also a political one, shaping electoral outcomes through local labor markets.

detail.title: Central Bank Digital Currency Adoption and Firms’ Cost of Capital
detail.abstract: Using a global sample of global firms from 2010 to 2023, we find that Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) adoption significantly reduces both the cost of equity and the cost of debt. Our conclusion is robust across various sensitivity analyses, including tests that mitigate potential endogeneity concerns. Mechanism tests show that CBDC adoption reduces information asymmetry, as evidenced by lower earnings management and improved analysts’ forecast quality. We further document that lower financing costs also translate into higher firm value and stronger investment and capital growth.

detail.abstract: This article analyzes the relationship between the analytical framework of economic development proposed by Nobel laureates Joel Mokyr , Philippe Aghion, and Peter Howitt , and the normative content of Title II of the 1991 Colombian Political Constitution , which establishes rights , guarantees , and duties. From an institutional perspective of development , the study evaluates whether the constitutional articles contained in this title provide sufficient normative and structural conditions to sustain long-term economic growth based on knowledge investment , innovation culture, creative destruction with social protection , and effective competition supported by antitrust regulation. Ultimately , the article contributes to the literature on constitutional economics by demonstrating that rights-based constitutional frameworks can function as foundational institutions for sustained innovation-led development , provided They are accompanied by active public policy , competition enforcement , and social protection mechanisms .

detail.abstract: This paper examines a November 2025 New York Magazine article on AI consciousness as a case study in how science journalism manufactures controversy where scientific consensus is reasonably clear. The article frames the question of whether large language models like ChatGPT might be conscious as an open scientific debate between roughly equivalent positions. In fact, one position-that LLMs lack any plausible mechanism for subjective experience-represents something much closer to the consensus among AI researchers, computational neuroscientists, and philosophers of mind, while the opposing view consists of speculative minority positions. The paper proceeds in four parts. First, it documents the journalistic failures: false balance between positions of unequal scientific standing, emotional priming through human-interest framing, and thin evidentiary support. Second, it examines the substantive question-why current LLM architecture provides no plausible mechanism for consciousness under any major theory of mind. Third, it exposes what the article systematically avoids: the commercial interests served by cultivating public uncertainty about AI sentience. The paper concludes that responsible science journalism on contested topics requires prioritizing consensus, avoiding false equivalence, and interrogating who benefits from manufactured doubt.

detail.abstract:
Aim
To analyse how New Zealand's 2025 restriction on initiating puberty blockers for people aged <18 was translated into delegated medicines regulation, and whether the public record reflects a differential evidentiary and governance standard.

Methods
We assembled a 67-document policy corpus and extracted a 32-field matrix from 12 core documents (statutory instruments, the Ministry of Health evidence brief, and key institutional/stakeholder texts). Using a seven-pillar "Regulatory Exceptionalism" framework, we analysed evidentiary framing, process signals, and rights/equity treatment.

Results
The restriction was made by regulation under s 105 of the Medicines Act 1981 (signed 17 Nov 2025; announced 19 Nov; gazetted 20 Nov; due to commence 19 Dec). The record treats evidentiary uncertainty as a categorical trigger for restricting initiation, bypassing routine governance tools used to manage off-label prescribing (professional standards, service governance, monitoring, and audit). Executive texts provide limited explicit engagement with proportionality, discrimination, and equity obligations, and leave review criteria and decision thresholds under-specified.

Conclusion
The decision is consistent with Regulatory Exceptionalism: higher evidentiary and governance standards are applied to a discrete population/indication than elsewhere in paediatrics. If uncertainty is the operative concern, proportionate alternatives include published MDT thresholds, registry-based monitoring, and time-limited policy with explicit review triggers rather than categorical prohibition.

title: The Future of Artificial Intelligence: Mathematical Evolution, Integration, and Global Impact

detail.title: The Future of Artificial Intelligence: Mathematical Evolution, Integration, and Global Impact
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is advancing at an unprecedented pace, driven by exponential increases in computational power, data availability, and algorithmic innovations. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of AI's future trajectory, combining theoretical models, empirical scaling trends, cross-domain case studies, and global strategic insights. We begin by developing rigorous mathematical models of AI growth, including power-law scaling laws that relate model performance to compute, model size, and dataset size. Using these models, we derive forecasting equations and discuss scenarios ranging from steady exponential progress to speculative paradigms such as artificial general intelligence (AGI) and human-AI symbiosis. We then validate these predictions with empirical data: original experiments and simulations illustrate how performance scales with compute, corroborating theoretical scaling laws with real-world trends. Visualizations of performance vs. compute and scaling curves demonstrate the striking exponential improvements observed in recent years. solving complex technical alignment problems and enacting thoughtful policies. We conclude with a discussion on long-term prospects, including the possibility of a human-AI symbiotic future where AI amplifies human intelligence, and we outline open challenges that will shape whether this future is beneficial. This work aims to serve as a definitive scholarly reference on AI's trajectory, providing a solid grounding in the mathematics of AI growth, validated trends, domain impacts, and the global landscape that will shape the future of intelligent machines.

detail.abstract: The convergence of global biomedical trends, shifting geopolitical supply chains, and domestic economic imperatives places Sakartvelo at a distinct historical inflection point. This report, commissioned to provide a comprehensive strategic roadmap, articulates the doctrine of Cliniversalism. This doctrine is not merely an economic policy but a civilizational strategy that reintegrates Sakartvelo's three-thousand-year lineage of healing-from the pharmacological techne of ancient Colchis to the bacteriophage innovations of the Soviet era-with a modern, hyper-liberalized private delivery system. The analysis conducted for this dossier reveals a bifurcated reality. On one hand, Sakartvelo possesses "blue ocean" assets that are structurally impossible for Western competitors to replicate rapidly: specifically, a living, regulatory-permissive ecosystem for bacteriophage therapy in an era of global Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR), and a massive stock of historic balneological infrastructure in Tskaltubo currently undergoing a billion-dollar revitalization. On the other hand, the system faces acute vulnerabilities. This report establishes that for Sakartvelo to succeed, it must reject the generic "medical tourism" model adopted by Turkey or Thailand, which competes on price commoditization.

detail.abstract: Economic and institutional performance is predominantly assessed using flow based indicators such as GDP, budget outlays, and annual output metrics. While useful for measuring short term activity, these measures provide limited insight into whether systems possess the structural and temporal conditions required to maintain or improve capability over time. This paper introduces R star, a universal Regeneration Index for evaluating the long horizon viability of institutional and economic systems. R star integrates structural features including decoupling from fragility cycles, alignment of capital with mission cycles, and realised regenerative recycling, with behavioural indicators capturing capability trends, volatility under shocks, and mission cycle completion. The index is normalised to a bounded scale in which negative values indicate degenerative systems, values near zero indicate fragile or stagnant architectures, and positive values indicate emergent or fully regenerative behaviour. Applications across health systems, climate adaptation, scientific research, and civic institutions demonstrate that R star can identify structural misalignment, anticipate capability decline, and distinguish regenerative architecture from temporary performance. At the national level, R star enables cross country comparison and shows that GDP is largely orthogonal to regenerative capacity, with some high income systems scoring poorly due to structural fragility. R star provides a general diagnostic metric for long horizon investment, governance design, and regenerative economic transition.

detail.abstract: Chemical separation procedures are very important in the manufacture of chemicals, energy, drugs, and cleaning up the environment, yet they are still among of the most energy-intensive processes in the business. Recent progress in artificial intelligence (AI) opens up new ways to make these systems more efficient, selective, and long-lasting. This article talks about how machine learning, data-driven modelling, and optimisation algorithms are starting to work with both old and new separation methods, such as distillation, membrane separations, adsorption, and hybrid processes. We talk about how AI improves process design by making it possible to quickly estimate how well a separation will work, adaptively control the process, and optimise multiple goals at once in difficult operating conditions. Spanish abstract: El trabajo analiza la contratación informática en el derecho argentino desde una perspectiva orientada a la protección de la continuidad operativa del usuario. Se observa que el software y los servicios tecnológicos se han integrado a la estructura productiva de las empresas, generando una dependencia técnica que exige adaptar la técnica contractual para evitar que una falla o interrupción comprometa el normal desarrollo del negocio. Se concluye que un contrato correctamente diseñado permite compatibilizar la protección del creador con la estabilidad económica del usuario, garantizando que la innovación tecnológica se consolide como fuente de competitividad y no de vulnerabilidad.

English abstract: This article analyzes IT contracting under Argentine private law, focusing on the protection of business continuity for users who rely on technological systems as essential components of their operations. Software and digital services create a technical dependency that requires contractual safeguards capable of preventing commercial disruption in case of failure or interruption. The study examines the duty of disclosure during pre-contractual negotiations, the legal scope of software usage rights, and the obligations of maintenance and support that ensure ongoing functionality. It also addresses risk-mitigation tools such as source code escrow, service level agreements, and data security requirements, which aim to preserve operational resilience. The analysis relies on the general principles of the Argentine Civil and Commercial Code and on local legal scholarship regarding IT contracts. The conclusion highlights that a well-structured contract can harmonize the provider’s intellectual property rights with the user’s economic stability, ensuring that technological innovation remains a source of competitiveness rather than vulnerability.

detail.abstract:
The Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) was the largest targeted business support program in U.S., yet its firm-level effects remain contested. I link administrative PPP and SBA 7(a) records to a near-universe panel of U.S. employer firms from Dun & Bradstreet, covering roughly 30 million establishments, and evaluate short-run impacts along employment, financial stress, and commercial credit risk. To address non-random take-up, I combine PSM with difference-in-differences on a balanced panel from March to September 2020 and exploit variation in loan holding duration.

PPP receipt raises employment by about 0.07 percent on average but improves failure-risk and delinquency-risk percentile rankings by roughly 1.2 and 3.2 points, respectively, with longer loan duration strengthening all three margins. Heterogeneity analysis shows that small–medium firms and borrowers with intermediate pre-crisis risk experience the largest gains, while micro, very large, and highly stressed firms benefit less. Firms without prior 7(a) borrowing relationships realize particularly large credit-score gains.

Overall, the evidence indicates that PPP functioned more as a balance-sheet and credit-risk backstop than as a powerful jobs program for the average treated firm. The results highlight how firm structure, pre-crisis financial health, and access to government-backed credit shape the effectiveness of large-scale emergency support.

detail.abstract:
This White Paper examines the structural limitations that constrain the enforceability of international commercial and sovereign mediated settlements. Although mediation offers versatility, confidentiality, and relationship preservation, its usefulness in high-value or politically sensitive disputes is restricted by the lack of automatic, neutral enforcement mechanisms. To bridge this gap, the paper proposes a Financial Enforcement Settlement (FES) framework that reconceptualises mediated settlements as instruments capable of immediate legal and financial effect. 

The FES model integrates three layers. First, a legal layer converts a mediated settlement into an enforceable title through mechanisms such as consent awards, homologated settlements, confessions of judgment, notarial deeds, or consent judgments. Second, a financial layer supplies liquidity and risk mitigation through independent undertakings, including standby letters of credit, guarantees, escrow structures, and political-risk insurance, that operate irrespective of the underlying merits. Third, a procedural layer establishes objective enforcement triggers supported by a clear certification process that verifies default by reference to agreed documents. 

By embedding enforcement within the settlement itself rather than deferring it to later litigation or arbitration, the FES framework reduces credit risk, prevents strategic default, improves sovereign compliance, and transforms mediated settlements into bankable and predictable instruments. This architecture aligns mediation with the expectations of global finance and state actors, thereby strengthening its viability in complex cross-border disputes.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether foreign aid focused on gender equality and women's empowerment reduces income inequality in recipient countries. While the impact of gender-sensitive aid on income inequality has not been widely researched, existing literature shows mixed results. We analyze gender-sensitive aid, government expenditure, economic growth, inflation rate, trade openness, and education as factors influencing income inequality, using data from the OECD and World Bank. Employing the generalized method of moments (GMM) technique, we study African countries that receive foreign aid from 2009 to 2022. Our results indicate that gendersensitive aid has a significant negative effect on income inequality. Therefore, governments in these countries should implement targeted policies and programs to effectively utilize gendersensitive aid in order to reduce income disparity.

title: The Suicide Region: Option Games and the Race to Artificial General Intelligence
affiliations: American University of the Middle East (AUM)

detail.title: The Suicide Region: Option Games and the Race to Artificial General Intelligence
detail.abstract:
Standard real options theory predicts delay in exercising the option to invest or deploy when extreme asset volatility or technological uncertainty is present. However, in the current race to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), sovereign actors are exhibiting behaviors contrary to theoretical predictions: the US and China are accelerating AI investment despite acknowledging the potential for global catastrophe from AGI misalignment. We resolve this puzzle by formalizing the AGI race as a continuous-time preemption game with endogenous existential risk. In our model, the cost of failure is no longer bounded only by the sunk cost of investment (I), but rather an additional systemic ruin parameter (D) that is correlated with development velocity and shared globally.

As the disutility of catastrophe is embedded in both players' payoffs, the risk term mathematically cancels out in the equilibrium indifference condition. This creates a "suicide region" in the investment space where competitive pressures force rational agents to deploy AGI systems early, despite a negative risk-adjusted net present value. Furthermore, we show that "warning shots" (sub-existential disasters) will fail to deter AGI acceleration, as the winner-takes-all nature of the race remains intact. The race can only be halted if the cost of ruin is internalized, making safety research a prerequisite for economic viability. We derive the critical private liability threshold required to restore the option value of waiting and propose mechanism design interventions that can better ensure safe AGI research and socially responsible deployment.

detail.abstract:
Procedural Cost Theory (PCT) is proposed as an initial conceptual framework for analyzing a category of costs that arise after contracts take effect. While Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) has extensively examined ex-ante governance choices and contract formation, a substantial portion of real-world frictions occurs during the execution, verification, and administrative processing of transactions. I refer to these phenomena collectively as procedural harm.

Examples include delays, administrative burdens, verification loops, consumer–firm disputes, multi-step service processes, and other institutional frictions that are difficult to characterize within existing TCE-based analyses. To provide preliminary structure for studying these issues, this paper introduces (1) Administrative Labor Substitution Cost (ALC) as a micro-level measure of procedural time burden, and (2) Procedural Harm Classification (PHC) as an early attempt to categorize common forms of procedural frictions.

PCT is presented here not as a finished theory but as a foundational proposal intended to delineate a new analytical space for post-transaction costs. The objective is to establish definitional clarity, motivate systematic study, and highlight conceptual gaps in current institutional economics. Further theoretical development will require integrating micro-level measurement, service-process analysis, and institutional design perspectives, which future work will elaborate.

Many organizations claim that they attract, retain, and motivate talent with an effective Total Rewards context, which is an integration of compensation & benefits, career development, recognition, and work-life balance. This is to understand if these elements of TR are managed under one function or by different functions within HR or outside the HR realm. The focus is to learn how the pandemic disrupted the business need and how Total Rewards evolved to support the change in the working environment.

The organizations could be offering the best Total Rewards in the market but it could still be irreverent if not communicated effectively to the workforce. The companies might be creating competitive Total Rewards structure but if the effectiveness of Total Rewards is not measured then how do they ensure if they can get the desired return from the investment made.

We connected with sixteen Total Rewards professionals working in IT companies in India to learn from them about their organizational Total Rewards philosophy and framework, how they are communicating/advertising TR to their employees, if they feel it is competitive, and whether they are measuring the effectiveness of their TR structure.

title: LLM-Driven Market Microstructure Representation Learning and Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Dynamics

detail.title: LLM-Driven Market Microstructure Representation Learning and Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified framework that combines market microstructure, large language model (LLM) representations, and game-theoretic reinforcement learning. High-frequency markets are modeled as strategic and adversarial systems in which heterogeneous agents interact through an LLM-induced representation of the limit order book. We formalize a representationdriven stochastic game, establish equilibrium existence and stability, and analyze how LLMinduced geometry shapes strategic incentives, volatility dynamics, and liquidity formation. We then outline an empirical framework based on message-level data and RL-based agents interacting with liquidity providers and takers in a realistic microstructure environment.

title: The DAWN Model: Dynamical Architecture of the Wave of Novelty

detail.title: The DAWN Model: Dynamical Architecture of the Wave of Novelty
detail.abstract: The DAWN Model proposes that cognitive activity oscillates between four dynamical phases-Compression, Expansion, Stabilization, and Recompression-governed by a linear differential relation between system compression C(t) and novelty input I(t). The model further predicts a system-specific recurrence threshold R, defined as the number of oscillatory cycles required for latent structure to become consciously interpretable under cognitive load. Preliminary introspective observation suggests R ≈ 77 for the human cognitive system, presented here explicitly as a falsifiable empirical prediction rather than a theoretical constant. DAWN offers a mathematically explicit, operationalizable, and testable framework for studying cognitive rhythm and the emergence of insight.

detail.title: Financial Fracture Mechanics: A Physics-Based Approach to Market Regime Switching and Liquidity Black Holes
detail.abstract: Traditional econometric models and machine learning algorithms often treat financial time series as stationary or linear processes, failing to account for phase transitions during liquidity crises. This paper introduces the 'Fracture Index', a novel econophysical framework that models financial assets as physical materials subject to stress and strain. By defining a 'Yield Point' based on localized price topology, we demonstrate that markets exhibit distinct 'Elastic' (Trending) and 'Plastic' (Mean Reverting) behaviors. Empirical backtesting on S&P 500 and high-frequency tactical data reveals that this physics-based approach significantly outperforms standard momentum strategies in detecting structural breaks, offering a Sharpe Ratio of >1.6 and acting as an effective early warning system for liquidity black holes.

title: PIME: Precision-Induced Macroeconomic Equilibrium: A Framework for Threshold Dynamics in High-Precision Capitalism

detail.title: PIME: Precision-Induced Macroeconomic Equilibrium: A Framework for Threshold Dynamics in High-Precision Capitalism
detail.abstract: This paper introduces Precision-Induced Macroeconomic Equilibrium (PIME), a framework in which informational precision, denoted σ, functions as a structural determinant of macroeconomic institutions. When σ is low, economies rely on uncertainty-management tools such as interest premia, unemployment buffers, precautionary markups, valuation volatility, leverage cycles, and stabilization policy. As σ rises-and especially once it crosses a threshold σ *-these institutions lose functional necessity, generating a non-linear regime shift driven by information resolution rather than policy discretion. Modern technological developments-including real-time analytics, digital identity, automated verification, supply-chain transparency, and instantaneous payments-substantially raise σ across sectors, making the σ ≥ σ * regime newly plausible. PIME unifies insights from Keynesian uncertainty, Minskyan instability, information economics (Akerlof-Stiglitz-Spence), New Keynesian expectations, MMT institutional analysis, and Hayekian coordination under a single scalar informational parameter. The framework explains observed patterns in digitally transparent sectors: declining real interest rates, narrowing price dispersion, reduced volatility, rent compression, and the weakening of stabilization tools. PIME provides the conceptual foundation for a broader research program on precision-driven macroeconomic evolution.

detail.title: Thermodynamic Phase Transitions in Financial Markets: Evidence from Fracture Analysis and Entropic Gravity
detail.abstract: Financial markets exhibit complex behaviors that traditional stochastic models fail to predict, particularly during liquidity crises. This paper proposes a unified 'Econophysical' theory that models asset prices as viscoelastic materials subject to stress, strain, and fatigue. We introduce two novel metrics: (1) The 'Fracture Index', which incorporates Young's Modulus to measure the elasticity of price trends, and (2) 'Entropic Gravity', which creates a dynamic event horizon based on systemic chaos. Empirical testing across multiple asset classes (S&P 500, Bitcoin, Gold) demonstrates that this framework successfully identifies phase transitions from elastic (trending) to plastic (crashing) regimes with >55% accuracy and a Sharpe Ratio exceeding 1.6. The results suggest that market crashes are not random outliers but mathematically inevitable consequences of accumulated material fatigue.

title: Real-Time Spectral Filtering in Financial Markets: A Micro-Application of the Marchenko-Pastur Law

detail.title: Real-Time Spectral Filtering in Financial Markets: A Micro-Application of the Marchenko-Pastur Law
detail.abstract: Random Matrix Theory (RMT) has proven that the majority of correlations in financial markets are indistinguishable from random noise. However, standard technical indicators (RSI, MACD) fail to differentiate between 'structural' price movements and 'thermal' noise. This paper introduces 'Eigen-Filter Pro', a lightweight algorithm that applies the Marchenko-Pastur Law to real-time assetbenchmark correlation matrices. By calculating a dynamic 'Noise Ceiling' (λ+), the algorithm systematically silences trading signals that lack spectral significance. Backtesting reveals that this 'Spectral Veto' mechanism reduces false positives by 40% in high-entropy regimes, effectively bridging the gap between theoretical Econophysics and retail algorithmic trading.
